Females of the Southern rough-winged swallow typically produce a single clutch of six eggs per nesting attempt [N_R_i = six eggs per nesting attempt], yielding just one brood per year [F_R_i = one brood per year] across their Neotropical range. This reproductive strategy, modest compared to many other hirundines, is tightly linked to the energetic constraints of aerial insectivory. Incubation period data from nests monitored in central Brazil indicate that eggs maintained at a constant temperature of 36 °C [T = 36 °C] require approximately 14 days [ab = approximately 14 days] to complete embryonic development, a duration consistent with the altricial mode of development typical of the genus Stelgidopteryx. The precise thermal regulation provided by the incubating adult is critical, as even small deviations from this temperature can prolong the incubation window by one to two additional days, as noted in comparative studies of related species. Field observations suggest that the incubation rhythm remains remarkably stable throughout the 14-day period.

Newly hatched chicks emerge weighing a mere 1.8 grams [Wwb = 1.8 grams], making them among the lighter altricial neonates among aerial insectivores of comparable adult body size. This minimal birth mass reflects the rapid growth trajectory that nestlings must achieve to fledge successfully within a constrained developmental window. During the first week post-hatching, the altricial nestlings are entirely dependent on the parents for brooding and provisioning, with both males and females participating fervently in food delivery. Mass gain is swift and linear, fueled by a diet of small dipterans, hymenopterans, and other soft-bodied arthropods captured on the wing. The nestlings attain an asymptotic weight of approximately 19 grams [Wwi = approximately 19 grams] before they begin to lose the fluffed juvenile down and develop the characteristic stiff rectrices and remiges that signal the approach of fledging. This asymptotic mass is notably lower than the average mass of an adult.

Under the metabolic conditions typical of an actively foraging adult (41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]), nestlings achieve fledging at approximately 19 days after hatching [tx = approximately 19 days after hatching]. This rapid nest departure, typical of many open-cup-nesting hirundines, minimizes the risk of predation during the vulnerable nestling stage. The post-fledging period remains risky, however, as flight feathers and foraging skills continue to develop. Following fledging, the juveniles attain puberty relatively quickly, with gonadal maturation occurring at roughly 57 days after hatching [tp = roughly 57 days after hatching] at a temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. This early maturation is ecologically advantageous in seasonal tropical environments, allowing young birds to exploit brief resource pulses and attempt breeding during the same season in which they were born. Field data from marked populations suggest that most individuals defer actual reproductive effort until they are approximately one year old.

First reproduction in the Southern rough-winged swallow is typically deferred until one year after hatching, corresponding to 365 days since birth [tR = 365 days since birth] at a temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. This interval aligns closely with the annual cycle of many tropical insectivores, which synchronize breeding with the onset of the wet season. The maximum recorded lifespan for a banded wild individual was 2154 days [am = 2154 days] since hatching, a relatively long duration for a small-bodied passerine at a temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. This longevity is likely facilitated by the species' low annual reproductive output and the relatively low predation rates experienced in its preferred cliff-face and bridge-nesting microhabitats. Senescence appears to occur gradually, with older individuals showing reduced fecundity and a slight decline in feather quality over successive molts, though detailed demographic studies remain scarce for this species.

Recent field studies have examined the relationship between ambient temperature and the provisioning behavior of breeding adults. When brooding nestlings at a core ambient temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C], parents maintain a high feeding rate to support the rapid mass gain required for successful fledging. A comparative analysis across several Hirundinidae species reveals that the Southern rough-winged swallow's maximum reproductive output is on the low end of the spectrum for the family, likely reflecting the energetic demands of prolonged foraging bouts in open country. The species' habitat preferences, which include riparian corridors and dry scrubland, expose it to considerable thermal variation, yet adults maintain remarkable thermoregulatory precision during incubation. Further work investigating the metabolic costs associated with this extended provisioning period would greatly enhance our understanding of life-history trade-offs in this understudied neotropical swallow.
